terms.definition: A number between 0 and 1 attached to a stated event under stated conditions. This lesson reads it as the relative frequency the event settles toward across many repetitions, which is what makes it checkable against a record.

The share of recorded trials in which an event occurred: the count of occurrences divided by the number of trials so far. It is an observed quantity that moves as a record grows, unlike the fixed probability it approaches.

A part measured against the whole it came from, expressed as a number between 0 and 1. Every probability computed by counting in this lesson is a proportion in this sense: the count of outcomes in the event over the count of outcomes in the group being counted inside.

alignment.note: PREM-QNT-003 defines a proportion as an equation asserting that two ratios are equal, such as a/b = c/d, and flags that data-analysis lessons use the word differently. This lesson introduces that second, statistical sense: a part measured against its whole. Both senses are standard and neither replaces the other; the opening scene names the collision before the word is used, and only the part-to-whole sense appears afterwards.

terms.definition: The set of all outcomes that a stated chance procedure can produce, with each outcome listed once. Drawing one of sixty study rows at random has a sample space of those sixty rows.

Any collection of outcomes from a sample space that a question is about, such as "the drawn participant ate late" or "the reading was 140 mg/dL or above". An event either occurs or does not on a given trial.

An event and the event that it does not occur. Together they cover the whole sample space and share no outcome, so their probabilities sum to 1 and the probability of one is one minus the probability of the other.

Two events that cannot both occur on the same trial, so the probability that both occur is zero and the probability that at least one occurs is the plain sum of their probabilities. Being in the early-dinner group and being in the late-dinner group is such a pair.

The rule for the probability that at least one of two events occurs: add their separate probabilities and subtract the probability that both occur, so that outcomes lying in both events are counted once rather than twice. The subtraction vanishes when the events are mutually exclusive.

The probability of one event among the outcomes where another event holds, written P(A given B) and equal to the probability that both occur divided by the probability of the conditioning event, which must be greater than zero. Conditioning discards every outcome outside the stated group and rescales what remains, so P(A given B) and P(B given A) are different questions with different answers.

The rule for the probability that two events both occur: multiply the probability of one by the conditional probability of the other given it. When the events are independent the conditional factor equals the unconditional probability and the rule reduces to the plain product of the two probabilities.

Two events whose joint probability equals the product of their separate probabilities, equivalently two events where learning that one occurred leaves the probability of the other unchanged. Independence is a property to be tested against the data or defended as a modelling assumption, never assumed for convenience.

The result that the observed relative frequency of an event across independent repeated trials converges to its probability as the number of trials grows. It constrains the share over a long record and says nothing about the next trial, so it never implies that a short-run deviation will be repaid.

The reasoning error of treating the probability of A given B as though it were the probability of B given A. In screening it turns a test's detection rate into a claim about a patient holding a positive result; in reading a study it turns a probability computed under a hypothesis into a probability of that hypothesis.
